title: Transactions, ACID, isolation levels, anomalies, MVCC
scopeHtml: Scope: ACID, anomalies, isolation levels per engine, MVCC for designers, locking, and transactions across services.

notes.title: What a transaction is
notes.html:
A transaction groups several reads and writes into one all-or-nothing unit that behaves as if it ran alone. Transferring 500 rupees: subtract from A, add to B. If the server dies between the two, you must not lose money. Transactions make "both or neither" a database guarantee instead of something every developer re-implements.

BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 500;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;   -- or ROLLBACK on any error

Worked example. At 2,000 transfers/s, each touching 2 rows, you expect about 4,000 row updates/s. With a crash roughly once a month, that is millions of transfers in flight over time; without transactions, some would end half-done. With a WAL, recovery replays or undoes them on restart.

Industry examples. Banks, Stripe's ledger, and every e-commerce checkout rely on transactions. Spanner and CockroachDB extend them across machines (distributed transactions). Many NoSQL stores (Cassandra) offer only single-partition atomicity; DynamoDB added TransactWriteItems (up to 100 items, confirm limit in docs).

Everyday analogy. Handing cash and receiving goods at a shop counter as one swap; you do not want to be left having paid but with no goods.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming each SQL statement is auto-transactional across several statements; only a single statement is atomic by default (autocommit).
  • Forgetting that a long transaction holds resources and blocks cleanup.

notes.title: ACID, each letter
notes.html:
ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

  • Atomicity: all or nothing. Implemented with an undo log or by never exposing uncommitted versions.
  • Consistency: the database moves between valid states (constraints, foreign keys, checks hold). Note: this "C" is largely the application's and constraints' job; it is not the same as CAP's consistency.
  • Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work. The strength is tunable (isolation levels).
  • Durability: once COMMIT returns, the data survives a crash. Implemented by writing the WAL and calling fsync before acknowledging.

Durability knobs and numbers. fsync on NVMe costs roughly 0.1 to 1 ms; on a network disk 1 to 5 ms. That caps single-connection commit rate at about 1,000 to 10,000 commits/s unless the engine uses group commit (batching many transactions into one fsync). Postgres: synchronous_commit = off risks losing the last few hundred milliseconds of commits (but never corrupts data) in exchange for speed. synchronous_standby_names makes commit wait for a replica, so a primary failure loses nothing but adds network latency. MySQL: innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 1 is full durability, 2 flushes about every second.

Industry examples. Postgres, MySQL/InnoDB, Oracle, SQL Server all implement ACID with a WAL. Redis with appendfsync everysec loses up to about one second of writes on a crash.

Everyday analogy. Signing a legal contract: not valid until fully signed (atomic), follows the law (consistent), not altered by someone else mid-signing (isolated), and filed in a safe afterwards (durable).

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up ACID consistency with CAP consistency.
  • Believing "committed" always means "on disk"; it depends on fsync settings and disk write caches.
  • Forgetting that atomicity does not mean "no errors"; it means rollback is clean.

notes.title: Concurrency problems (anomalies)
notes.html:
Anomalies are the strange results you get when transactions interleave without enough isolation. Learn them by name and a tiny example.

Anomaly What happens
Dirty read You read data another transaction wrote but has not committed (may be rolled back).
Non-repeatable read You read a row twice in one transaction and get different values because someone committed in between.
Phantom read You run the same range query twice and new rows appear (or vanish) because someone inserted/deleted matching rows.
Lost update Two transactions read the same value, both modify it, the second write overwrites the first.
Write skew Two transactions read overlapping data, each writes a different row, and together they break a rule neither broke alone. 
Write skew (on-call doctors; rule: at least one must stay on call)
T1: SELECT count(*) WHERE on_call   -> 2
T2: SELECT count(*) WHERE on_call   -> 2
T1: UPDATE alice SET on_call=false  (sees 2, thinks 1 remains)
T2: UPDATE bob   SET on_call=false  (sees 2, thinks 1 remains)
COMMIT both -> nobody on call.   Different rows written, so no row-lock conflict.
Lost update (counter)
T1: read 10   T2: read 10
T1: write 11  T2: write 11     -> should be 12

Fixes for lost update: atomic update SET n = n + 1; SELECT ... FOR UPDATE; optimistic version column (UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND version=?); or a serializable isolation level.

Industry examples. Write skew is the classic issue behind double-booking of meeting rooms, seats, and usernames. Real incidents: double-spent wallet balances, oversold inventory, duplicate coupon redemptions.

Everyday analogy. Two people editing the same shared document offline and both saving: the later save silently wipes the first person's change.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking row locks stop write skew; they do not when different rows are written.
  • Treating phantom reads as "just non-repeatable reads"; they involve rows that did not exist before.
  • Not knowing a fix for lost updates.

notes.title: Isolation levels
notes.html:
The SQL standard defines four isolation levels, each allowing fewer anomalies. Stronger isolation means fewer surprises and lower concurrency.

Level Dirty read Non-repeatable Phantom Notes
Read Uncommitted Possible Possible Possible Rarely used
Read Committed No Possible Possible Postgres default, Oracle default
Repeatable Read No No Standard allows; Postgres snapshot prevents MySQL InnoDB default
Serializable No No No As if one at a time

Real engines differ from the textbook table, and interviews love this:

  • Postgres Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation: it prevents phantoms but still allows write skew. Postgres Serializable uses SSI (serializable snapshot isolation), detecting dangerous patterns and aborting one transaction with a serialization error; the app must retry.
  • MySQL InnoDB Repeatable Read uses gap and next-key locks to block phantoms for locking reads; plain consistent reads use a snapshot.
  • Oracle has no true Repeatable Read; its SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation.
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- ... reads and writes ...
COMMIT;   -- may fail with SQLSTATE 40001; retry the whole transaction

Decision gravity. Setting the default level is a two-way door in code, but changing it in an existing system can surface new deadlocks and retries; hard to test. Defaulting to Read Committed and fixing specific hot spots with FOR UPDATE, atomic updates or constraints is the common pragmatic path. Money-critical invariants (no negative balance, no double booking) deserve Serializable or explicit locks plus a unique constraint.

Worked example. Booking the last seat: SELECT seats_left then UPDATE. Under Read Committed two requests both see 1 and both succeed (oversell). Fixes: UPDATE seats SET left = left - 1 WHERE id=? AND left > 0 and check the affected row count; or a unique constraint on (flight, seat_no).

Industry examples. Stripe documents using idempotency keys plus database constraints; Postgres teams commonly run Read Committed with explicit locking; Spanner and CockroachDB default to serializable.

Everyday analogy. Rules for a shared kitchen: no rules (chaos), no touching others' half-cooked food, a reserved shelf per cook, or only one cook at a time.

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting the textbook table without knowing the engine-specific differences.
  • Forgetting that Serializable needs a retry loop in the app.
  • Believing Repeatable Read in Postgres prevents all anomalies (write skew still happens).

notes.title: MVCC for designers
notes.html:
MVCC (multi-version concurrency control) keeps several versions of each row so readers never block writers and writers never block readers. Each transaction sees a consistent snapshot as of its start (or statement start for Read Committed).

How Postgres does it: every row version (tuple) carries xmin (the transaction that created it) and xmax (the one that deleted or updated it). An UPDATE inserts a new version and marks the old one with xmax. A snapshot lists which transaction IDs are visible. Old, no-longer-visible versions are dead tuples removed later by VACUUM.

How InnoDB does it: the latest version lives in the clustered index; older versions are reconstructed from undo logs (rollback segment) when a reader needs them. A purge thread removes undo records no longer needed.

Row id=1 (Postgres heap)
v1 balance=100 xmin=100 xmax=205    <- dead after T205 commits
v2 balance=150 xmin=205 xmax=0      <- current
Reader with snapshot taken before T205 still sees v1.

Designer implications:

  • Long-running transactions are expensive. They pin old versions, so vacuum/purge cannot clean up; tables bloat, indexes grow, queries slow down. Metric: oldest transaction age, pg_stat_activity.xact_start, InnoDB "history list length" climbing.
  • idle in transaction sessions are a classic cause. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
  • Write-write conflicts still lock rows: two updates of the same row serialize.
  • Hot rows (a global counter updated by every request) become a bottleneck; shard the counter or use Redis.
  • Transaction ID wraparound (Postgres): 32-bit transaction IDs mean the database must "freeze" old rows via vacuum; if autovacuum fails to keep up, Postgres eventually forces a protective shutdown. Several large companies have publicly written post-mortems on this.
-- Find long transactions
SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS age, state, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 5;

Worked example. A table with 10M rows updated at 5,000 rows/s creates 5,000 dead tuples/s. If one forgotten transaction holds a snapshot open for an hour, 18M dead tuples accumulate and cannot be reclaimed; table size may double and scans slow.

Industry examples. Postgres, Oracle, InnoDB, CockroachDB, Spanner all use MVCC. Sentry and others have written about Postgres wraparound scares; Uber's Postgres-to-MySQL story referenced Postgres MVCC and index update behaviour (debated).

Everyday analogy. A shared Google Doc with version history: you can keep reading the version you opened while others save new ones; old versions are cleaned up only when nobody is still reading them.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying MVCC means "no locks at all".
  • Ignoring vacuum/purge and bloat in the design.
  • Leaving a transaction open across an external HTTP call.

notes.title: Locks, deadlocks and optimistic vs pessimistic control
notes.html:
Pessimistic control locks first; optimistic control checks at commit.

  • Pessimistic: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the rows until commit. Safe under contention, but holds locks and risks deadlocks.
  • Optimistic: read a version column, update with WHERE version = :v, check rows affected = 1; if 0, retry. Best when conflicts are rare.
  • SKIP LOCKED: let workers claim jobs without waiting.
-- Pessimistic
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM inventory WHERE sku='A1' FOR UPDATE;
UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku='A1';
COMMIT;

-- Optimistic
UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1, version = version + 1
WHERE sku='A1' AND version = 17 AND qty > 0;   -- check rowcount

-- Work queue without blocking
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status='NEW'
ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

Deadlock: T1 holds A and waits for B; T2 holds B and waits for A. The database detects the cycle (Postgres checks after deadlock_timeout, default 1 s) and aborts one. Prevent by always locking rows in a consistent order (for example by ascending id) and keeping transactions short.

Worked example. Flash sale of 100 units, 5,000 concurrent buyers on the same SKU. Pessimistic locking serialises all 5,000 on one row (each holding the lock maybe 5 ms = about 200 per second max). Optimistic with retries collapses under contention. Better: UPDATE ... SET qty=qty-1 WHERE qty>0 (single statement, brief lock), or pre-allocate stock into a Redis counter / queue.

Industry examples. Ticketing and flash-sale systems (BookMyShow, Ticketmaster style) use short atomic updates, queues and virtual waiting rooms to protect the DB; Rails and Hibernate popularised optimistic @Version.

Everyday analogy. Pessimistic: reserve the meeting room before discussing. Optimistic: discuss, then check at the end that nobody else changed the agenda.

Common interview traps.

  • Holding FOR UPDATE while calling a payment API.
  • Locking rows in inconsistent order across code paths.
  • Using optimistic locking under heavy contention (retry storms).

notes.title: Transactions across services: sagas, 2PC and outbox
notes.html:
A single database gives ACID; once you split data across services or shards, you need other patterns.

  • Two-phase commit (2PC): a coordinator asks all participants to prepare (promise to commit), then tells all to commit. Atomic, but blocks if the coordinator dies after prepare, and holds locks across the network. Used inside Spanner/CockroachDB (with replicated coordinators) and XA transactions.
  • Saga: a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it (refund, release stock). Eventually consistent; temporary intermediate states are visible.
  • Transactional outbox: write the business row and an "event to publish" row in the same local transaction; a relay (CDC, e.g. Debezium, or a poller) publishes the event to Kafka. This removes the "saved to DB but failed to publish" gap.
  • Idempotency keys: make retries safe; store the key with a unique constraint.
// Idempotent payment write: duplicate retries hit the unique constraint
// CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON payments (idempotency_key);
int rows = jdbc.update(
  "INSERT INTO payments(idempotency_key, order_id, amount) VALUES (?,?,?) " +
  "ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING", key, orderId, amount);
if (rows == 0) return loadExisting(key);   // already processed

Worked example. Order flow: reserve stock (5 ms), charge card (800 ms external), create shipment (20 ms). A distributed 2PC would hold stock locks for the whole 800 ms; a saga commits each step locally and, if the charge fails, runs "release stock".

Decision gravity. Moving from one database to many services (and sagas) is a one-way door in complexity: you trade guarantees for independence. If you can keep related data in one database (and one shard key), do; it is far simpler.

Industry examples. Uber's Cadence/Temporal for workflows and sagas; Stripe's idempotency keys on every POST; Amazon's order pipeline uses compensations; Debezium outbox pattern is widespread with Kafka.

Everyday analogy. Planning a trip with separate bookings: if the hotel fails after the flight is booked, you cancel the flight (compensation) rather than expecting one magical atomic booking.

Common interview traps.

  • Dual-writing to DB and Kafka without an outbox.
  • Claiming sagas are ACID; they lack isolation.
  • Forgetting idempotency on retries and compensations.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A transaction is all-or-nothing, as if run alone; autocommit protects only single statements.
  • ACID: atomicity (undo), consistency (constraints, not CAP), isolation (tunable), durability (WAL plus fsync, group commit, replica ack).
  • Anomalies: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update, write skew; know the example and the fix for each.
  • Isolation levels differ per engine: Postgres Read Committed default, Repeatable Read is snapshot (allows write skew), Serializable uses SSI with retries; InnoDB default Repeatable Read with gap locks.
  • MVCC: readers do not block writers via row versions (xmin/xmax or undo logs); cost is vacuum/purge, bloat, long transactions, wraparound.
  • Prefer atomic single-statement updates, constraints and short transactions; use FOR UPDATE, optimistic versions or SKIP LOCKED deliberately; lock in consistent order.
  • Across services use sagas, outbox and idempotency keys; avoid 2PC unless the platform provides it.

questions.promptHtml: Explain ACID. How does a database actually guarantee durability when COMMIT returns?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks you know the guarantees are implemented mechanisms with a cost, not slogans.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Atomicity is all or nothing, done with an undo log or by never exposing uncommitted versions. Consistency means constraints hold, and is mostly the schema and the application's job, not CAP consistency. Isolation means concurrent transactions do not see half-finished work, at a tunable level. Durability means that once COMMIT returns the data survives a crash: the engine appends to the write-ahead log and calls fsync before acknowledging.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: FLOWSVG0X An fsync costs about 0.1 to 1 ms on NVMe and 1 to 5 ms on a network disk, which would cap one connection at roughly 1,000 to 10,000 commits/s. Engines use group commit: many concurrent transactions share one fsync. Knobs: Postgres synchronous_commit = off can lose the last few hundred ms of commits on a crash but never corrupts data; synchronous_standby_names makes commit wait for a replica; MySQL innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 1 is full durability, 2 flushes about once per second. Disk write caches without power protection can make "committed" not really on disk.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Confusing ACID consistency with CAP consistency.
  • Believing "committed" always means "on disk".
  • Thinking atomicity means "no errors" rather than "clean rollback".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the WAL written before pages? -> It is sequential and small; data pages can be flushed later and rebuilt from the log after a crash.
  2. What is group commit? -> Batching several transactions' log records into one fsync, raising throughput at a small latency cost.
  3. How do you lose zero data on primary failure? -> Synchronous replication to at least one standby, accepting extra commit latency.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists the four letters. The senior ties durability to fsync cost and configuration, names the C confusion, and can state what is lost under each setting.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team set synchronous_commit=off for speed and later discovered a crash had dropped about 300 ms of acknowledged payments.

questions.promptHtml: Explain lost update and write skew with an example each. Why doesn't a row lock fix write skew, and what does?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many "double booking" bugs are write skew. Seniors recognise the pattern and choose the right fix.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Lost update: two transactions read the same value, both modify it, the second write overwrites the first. Write skew: two transactions read overlapping data, each updates a different row, and together they break a rule neither broke alone. Row locks do not help write skew because there is no shared row to lock; I need Serializable isolation, a lock on the shared parent or a constraint that makes the invariant checkable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Lost update (counter)            Write skew (on-call doctors, rule: >=1 on call)
T1: read 10   T2: read 10        T1: count on_call -> 2   T2: count on_call -> 2
T1: write 11  T2: write 11       T1: alice off            T2: bob off
=> 11, should be 12              => nobody on call; different rows, no conflict

Lost update fixes: atomic SET n = n + 1, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, an optimistic version column, or Serializable. Write skew fixes: Serializable (Postgres SSI aborts one with SQLSTATE 40001, app retries), locking a parent row (the "shift" row) that both transactions must update, or a database constraint/exclusion constraint where possible. Typical victims: meeting-room double booking, seat booking, username claims.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying FOR UPDATE on the rows read fixes write skew when the rows written differ and were not locked.
  • Treating phantoms as just non-repeatable reads: they involve rows that did not exist before.
  • Using Repeatable Read in Postgres and assuming it is serializable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which isolation levels prevent lost update? -> Postgres Repeatable Read aborts the second writer with a serialization error; Read Committed does not, but atomic updates or FOR UPDATE do.
  2. How would a unique constraint help double-booking? -> A unique (room, slot) makes the second insert fail.
  3. What must the app do on Serializable? -> Retry the whole transaction on 40001.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer names the anomalies. The senior shows the interleaving, explains why locks miss write skew and picks among Serializable, parent-row lock and constraint by contention and cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A booking system oversold meeting rooms for months until a unique constraint on room and slot replaced check-then-insert.

questions.contextHtml:
A ticketing service sells the last seats. Postgres, default isolation. Code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
@Transactional
public void book(long eventId, int qty) {
    int left = jdbc.queryForObject(
        "SELECT seats_left FROM events WHERE id = ?", Integer.class, eventId);
    if (left >= qty) {
        jdbc.update("UPDATE events SET seats_left = ? WHERE id = ?", left - qty, eventId);
        jdbc.update("INSERT INTO tickets(event_id, qty) VALUES (?, ?)", eventId, qty);
    } else throw new SoldOutException();
}
@Transactional
fun book(eventId: Long, qty: Int) {
    val left = jdbc.queryForObject(
        "SELECT seats_left FROM events WHERE id = ?", Int::class.java, eventId)!!
    if (left >= qty) {
        jdbc.update("UPDATE events SET seats_left = ? WHERE id = ?", left - qty, eventId)
        jdbc.update("INSERT INTO tickets(event_id, qty) VALUES (?, ?)", eventId, qty)
    } else throw SoldOutException()
}

Event capacity 500. After a sale burst: 523 tickets issued, seats_left = -3 in some rows and 11 in others. The team proposes SERIALIZABLE globally.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug, and what is the best fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in a transaction" (it already is) or "make everything Serializable" without discussing retries and throughput.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the traffic per event (hot row)? Can a request buy several seats? Is there an existing unique key per seat? Is the final count authoritative from tickets or from seats_left?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a CHECK (seats_left >= 0) constraint so overselling fails loudly; stop sales for affected events and reconcile with refunds.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Read-then-write under Read Committed: both transactions read the same left and write stale values (lost update). (b) Ticket insert not tied to the counter. (c) Retries doubling the effect.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare sum(qty) in tickets against capacity minus seats_left; replay two concurrent requests in a test with pg_sleep between read and write.
  5. Root cause: seats_left is computed in app memory from a read that is stale by the time of the write; Read Committed allows this lost update.
  6. Fix: Make the check and the decrement one atomic statement:
UPDATE events SET seats_left = seats_left - :qty
WHERE id = :id AND seats_left >= :qty;   -- check rows affected == 1

Insert the ticket only if one row was updated, in the same transaction. For per-seat inventory use a unique (event_id, seat_no). 7. Prevention: A DB constraint as a safety net, a concurrent test, and a review rule against read-modify-write in application code. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Global Serializable would work but forces retry logic everywhere and lowers throughput on hot rows. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is also correct but holds the lock longer than the single atomic UPDATE.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 50,000 buyers hit one event in a minute? -> The row becomes a hot spot; use a queue, waiting room or pre-allocated counters.
  • Optimistic version instead? -> Works under low contention; under a flash sale retries storm.
  • MySQL InnoDB? -> Same bug under its default Repeatable Read, since the plain SELECT is a snapshot read.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An oversold concert cost refunds and goodwill; the fix was a single conditional UPDATE plus a check constraint, a five-line change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the framework or adds a Java lock.
  • Hire: atomic conditional UPDATE and affected-rows check.
  • Strong hire: constraint safety net, hot-row mitigation, compares optimistic, pessimistic and Serializable.

questions.contextHtml:
A scheduling app requires at least 1 nurse on every shift. Postgres at REPEATABLE READ. Code in a transaction:

SELECT count(*) FROM assignments WHERE shift_id = 9 AND status = 'ON';
-- app: if count >= 2 then
UPDATE assignments SET status = 'OFF' WHERE shift_id = 9 AND nurse_id = :me;

Audit finds 14 shifts last month with zero nurses on duty. Logs show two requests overlapping by milliseconds each time. Developer: "Repeatable Read gives a stable snapshot, so this cannot happen."
questions.promptHtml: Explain what happened and how to fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Agrees Repeatable Read is safe, or adds FOR UPDATE only on the row being changed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the invariant "at least one" per shift only, or more rules? What is the contention per shift? Can the app retry?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a periodic check job that alerts on empty shifts and pages a manager; manually fix the 14 shifts.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Write skew: both transactions see count 2 in their own snapshots, each turns off a different row. (b) App bug in the count condition. (c) Clock or retry duplicates.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with two sessions: both BEGIN, both SELECT count, both UPDATE, both COMMIT. Check the log for overlapping timestamps.
  5. Root cause: Postgres Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation. It prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms but still allows write skew because the two writes touch different rows and never conflict.
  6. Fix: Option 1: run these transactions at SERIALIZABLE; Postgres SSI aborts one with 40001 and the app retries. Option 2: lock a row both must touch, e.g. SELECT ... FROM shifts WHERE id = 9 FOR UPDATE first, serialising per shift. Option 3: lock the rows read: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on all ON assignments for the shift.
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- check and update
COMMIT;  -- on SQLSTATE 40001: retry the whole transaction
  1. Prevention: Name the invariants in design docs, add a concurrency test with two threads, and add a retry wrapper.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Serializable adds aborts under contention; the parent lock is simpler and predictable if contention is per shift. I would not rely on application-level synchronized, which fails across instances.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• On MySQL InnoDB Repeatable Read? -> Plain SELECT is a snapshot read, so use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (gap/next-key locks) or Serializable.
  • Why does Serializable have a retry loop? -> SSI detects dangerous dependency patterns and aborts, so the app must re-run.
  • Could a constraint express the rule? -> Not easily with a plain constraint; a trigger plus lock or a counter row works.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A hospital roster app had a month of zero-coverage shifts from this exact pattern; locking the shift row fixed it with no retry code.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: insists the snapshot protects it.
  • Hire: names write skew and uses Serializable with retry or a lock.
  • Strong hire: compares options, notes engine differences, adds detection and tests.

questions.contextHtml:
A wallet service transfers money between accounts. Under load you see:

ERROR: deadlock detected
DETAIL: Process 4121 waits for ShareLock on transaction 99812; blocked by process 4377.
        Process 4377 waits for ShareLock on transaction 99811; blocked by process 4121.
HINT: See server log for query details.

about 40 per minute at 2,000 transfers/s. The code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
@Transactional
void transfer(long from, long to, long amt) {
    jdbc.update("UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - ? WHERE id = ?", amt, from);
    jdbc.update("UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + ? WHERE id = ?", amt, to);
}
@Transactional
fun transfer(from: Long, to: Long, amt: Long) {
    jdbc.update("UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - ? WHERE id = ?", amt, from)
    jdbc.update("UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + ? WHERE id = ?", amt, to)
}

A teammate wants to raise deadlock_timeout to reduce the errors.
questions.promptHtml: Why do the deadlocks happen and how do you eliminate them?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Raises the timeout or retries blindly. Does not see the opposing lock order between A to B and B to A transfers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are there other code paths that touch multiple accounts (fees, batch)? Are balance checks needed (no negative)? What is the transaction duration?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Retry on deadlock (SQLSTATE 40P01) with backoff, since the database aborts one victim; this is a stopgap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Inconsistent lock order: T1 transfers A to B (locks A then B) while T2 transfers B to A (locks B then A). (b) Long transactions widen the window. (c) Foreign key or index locks.
  4. How I'd verify each: Postgres log with log_lock_waits, pg_locks joined with pg_stat_activity; MySQL SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS latest deadlock section.
  5. Root cause: Cycle in waits: each transaction holds one row lock and waits for the other. The database detects it after deadlock_timeout (1 s default in Postgres) and kills one.
  6. Fix: Always lock in a global order, for example ascending account id:
SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id IN (:from, :to) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - :amt WHERE id = :from AND bal >= :amt;
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + :amt WHERE id = :to;

Then deadlock between two transfers is impossible. Keep transactions short and keep the retry as a safety net. 7. Prevention: A lint/review rule: multi-row locks sorted by key; a stress test with random pairs; alert on deadlock count. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Raising deadlock_timeout just makes victims wait longer. Sorting adds one locking query, which is cheap. Avoid external calls inside the transaction.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Transfer A to A? -> Handle explicitly: the same row twice.
  • Hot account (merchant) receives most transfers? -> Serialises on that row; use a ledger of entries and aggregate balances.
  • Does optimistic locking avoid deadlocks? -> It avoids lock waits but creates retries under contention.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payments team cut deadlock errors from dozens per minute to zero by sorting ids, with a three-line change and a stress test.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises timeouts.
  • Hire: identifies lock-order cycle and sorts locks.
  • Strong hire: also retry strategy, hot-row design and observability.

questions.contextHtml:
A Postgres orders database (10M-row hot table, 5,000 updates/s) slowly degrades over a week: table size grew from 20 GB to 55 GB, queries slow, autovacuum is running constantly but not finishing its work.

SELECT pid, now()-xact_start AS age, state, left(query,40)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 3;
 pid  |   age    |        state        | left
 8812 | 6 days   | idle in transaction | SELECT * FROM config WHERE ...
 9020 | 00:00:41 | active              | UPDATE orders SET ...

pg_stat_user_tables: orders  n_live_tup=10.2M  n_dead_tup=412M

A teammate wants to run VACUUM FULL orders immediately.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and how do you respond?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: VACUUM FULL at peak (takes an exclusive lock and blocks the table) or increase autovacuum workers; neither addresses the cause.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who owns pid 8812 (a service connection, a BI tool, a forgotten psql)? Do we have replicas with hot_standby_feedback? Is there any logical replication slot lagging? What is the txid age (wraparound risk)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Terminate the idle-in-transaction session (pg_terminate_backend(8812)) after confirming it is safe. Also check replication slots and prepared transactions, which pin old snapshots too.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) An open old transaction pins the snapshot horizon so vacuum cannot remove dead tuples. (b) A lagging replication slot or standby feedback does the same. (c) Autovacuum settings too lax for 5,000 updates/s.
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_stat_activity (xact_start, backend_xmin), pg_replication_slots (xmin, restart_lsn), pg_prepared_xacts, and n_dead_tup trend after the kill.
  5. Root cause: MVCC keeps old versions for any snapshot that might still need them. 5,000 updates/s create 5,000 dead tuples/s; six days pinned yields hundreds of millions that cannot be reclaimed, causing bloat in the table and indexes and slower scans.
  6. Fix: Short term: end the session; autovacuum can then clean (space is reused, not returned to the OS). To reclaim disk use pg_repack (online) rather than VACUUM FULL, outside peak. Long term: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, statement_timeout, app fix so no transaction stays open across a request, and per-table autovacuum tuning (lower scale factor for hot tables).
  7. Prevention: Alert on oldest transaction age and n_dead_tup, track age(datfrozenxid) for wraparound, and review transaction boundaries in code (no open transaction across HTTP calls).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: VACUUM FULL takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the duration (hours on 55 GB). Killing sessions is safe only after confirming nothing needs them. Setting a short idle timeout may break slow clients; pick it from measured data.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does InnoDB show the same problem? -> Long transactions pin undo logs; history list length climbs.
  • Does this relate to wraparound? -> Yes, vacuum that cannot freeze rows pushes toward 32-bit transaction ID wraparound, which can force a protective shutdown.
  • Could a replica query cause it? -> With hot_standby_feedback on, yes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A forgotten notebook session in a transaction doubled a table and slowed a checkout path for days; one timeout setting prevented it from recurring.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: VACUUM FULL or more workers.
  • Hire: finds the long idle transaction and its effect on vacuum.
  • Strong hire: checks slots and replicas, uses pg_repack, adds timeouts and monitors wraparound.

questions.promptHtml: The SQL standard has four isolation levels. How do Postgres and MySQL InnoDB actually behave at Read Committed, Repeatable Read and Serializable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The textbook table is not what engines do. Seniors know the real behaviour and its traps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Postgres defaults to Read Committed, where each statement sees a fresh snapshot. Its Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation: no phantoms, but write skew is still possible. Its Serializable uses SSI, which detects dangerous patterns and aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001, so the app must retry. InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read, with a consistent snapshot for plain reads and next-key/gap locks for locking reads. Oracle has no true Repeatable Read and its SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Level Dirty Non-repeatable Phantom Notes
Read Uncommitted possible possible possible rarely used
Read Committed no possible possible Postgres and Oracle default
Repeatable Read no no standard allows; Postgres snapshot prevents InnoDB default
Serializable no no no as if one at a time 
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- reads and writes
COMMIT;   -- may fail with SQLSTATE 40001: retry the whole transaction

Stronger isolation means fewer surprises, more aborts or waits. A pragmatic approach: default to Read Committed, then protect specific invariants with atomic updates, FOR UPDATE, constraints or Serializable for the critical transactions.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reciting the textbook table without engine specifics.
  • Forgetting that Serializable needs a retry loop.
  • Believing Postgres Repeatable Read prevents all anomalies.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which anomaly survives Postgres Repeatable Read? -> Write skew.
  2. How does InnoDB stop phantoms? -> Next-key (record plus gap) locks on locking reads.
  3. What do Spanner and CockroachDB default to? -> Serializable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer recites the table. The senior knows per-engine behaviour, the retry requirement, and how to choose per invariant instead of one global level.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A migration from MySQL to Postgres surfaced new lost updates because code relied on InnoDB lock behaviour that Postgres Read Committed does not provide.

questions.promptHtml: How does MVCC work in Postgres versus InnoDB, and what are the design consequences?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: MVCC explains bloat, long-transaction pain and wraparound; designers must anticipate them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: MVCC keeps several versions of a row so readers do not block writers. Postgres stores each version in the heap with xmin (creator) and xmax (deleter), and an UPDATE inserts a new version; VACUUM removes dead ones. InnoDB keeps the latest version in the clustered index and rebuilds older versions from undo logs, with a purge thread cleaning them. The design consequences: long transactions pin old versions and cause bloat, hot rows still serialise writers, and Postgres needs vacuum to keep ahead of transaction ID wraparound.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Row id=1 (Postgres heap)
v1 balance=100 xmin=100 xmax=205   <- dead once T205 commits
v2 balance=150 xmin=205 xmax=0     <- current
A reader whose snapshot predates T205 still sees v1.

Numbers: 5,000 updates/s create 5,000 dead tuples/s; an hour-long open transaction pins about 18M of them. Metrics to watch: oldest transaction age (pg_stat_activity.xact_start), n_dead_tup, InnoDB history list length. Postgres transaction IDs are 32-bit, so old rows must be frozen by vacuum; if autovacuum cannot keep up the database eventually refuses writes to protect itself.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "MVCC means no locks": two writers to the same row still wait.
  • Opening a transaction, then calling an external HTTP API.
  • Ignoring autovacuum tuning on hot tables.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a HOT update? -> A Postgres optimisation where an update that changes no indexed column stays on the same page without new index entries.
  2. How do you handle a global counter row? -> Shard it into N rows or move it to Redis; write contention is not solved by MVCC.
  3. What set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout for? -> Killing sessions that hold snapshots open without work.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "readers do not block writers". The senior explains versions, vacuum/purge cost, bloat and wraparound, and designs transaction boundaries and counters accordingly.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Several companies have published post-mortems about Postgres wraparound scares and bloat from forgotten transactions.

questions.contextHtml:
A flash sale of 100 units of one SKU expects 5,000 concurrent buyers. The current code uses pessimistic locking:

BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM inventory WHERE sku = 'A1' FOR UPDATE;
-- call pricing service (about 30 ms)
UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'A1';
COMMIT;

During last sale: throughput about 25 purchases/s, p99 latency 14 s, DB connection pool exhausted, many 500s. A teammate proposes optimistic locking with a version column instead.
questions.promptHtml: How do you redesign it to survive 5,000 buyers?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Switches to optimistic locking and retries. Under heavy contention that creates a retry storm: nearly all attempts fail and re-run.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must buyers see an instant yes/no? Is stock strictly 100 (no oversell)? Is payment synchronous? Can we use a queue or waiting room?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap concurrency at the edge and shed excess with a 429 or waiting room, so the DB sees a bounded load.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The lock is held across a 30 ms external call, so max throughput is about 1000/30 = 33/s, close to the observed 25/s. (b) Pool exhaustion cascades: connections wait on the lock. (c) Optimistic retries would multiply load.
  4. How I'd verify each: Lock wait metrics (pg_locks, pg_stat_activity wait events), per-transaction duration, pool wait time.
  5. Root cause: All buyers serialise on one row, and the lock is held for the whole transaction including a network call.
  6. Fix: Take the call out of the lock and make the decrement one atomic statement:
UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'A1' AND qty > 0;  -- rows affected 1 = success

The lock is held for well under a millisecond. For 100 units, pre-load stock into a Redis counter or a queue of tokens; reserve first, pay after, release on timeout (a small saga). Use a waiting room to smooth the 5,000. 7. Prevention: Load test the hot SKU path, alert on lock waits and pool saturation, and keep external calls outside transactions. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Optimistic locking suits rare conflicts; here 4,900 of 5,000 would lose and retry. The Redis counter adds a reconciliation step with the database. I would not hold FOR UPDATE across the pricing call.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Buyer reserves, never pays? -> Reservation with TTL and a release job.
  • Redis loses the counter? -> Rebuild from the database ledger; the DB is the source of truth.
  • Multiple SKUs in one cart? -> Lock in sorted SKU order or reserve each atomically with compensation.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sale collapsed at 25 orders/s because the lock spanned a pricing call; moving the call outside and using a conditional UPDATE reached about 2,000/s on the same hardware.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: optimistic retry or bigger DB.
  • Hire: atomic conditional UPDATE and shorter transaction.
  • Strong hire: throughput math, queue or waiting room, reservation TTL and reconciliation.

questions.contextHtml:
An order service writes the order to Postgres, then publishes OrderPlaced to Kafka:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
@Transactional
public void place(Order o) {
    orderRepo.save(o);
    kafka.send("orders", o.id(), o.toEvent());   // fire and forget
}
@Transactional
fun place(o: Order) {
    orderRepo.save(o)
    kafka.send("orders", o.id(), o.toEvent())   // fire and forget
}

Incident: during a Kafka broker restart 0.4 percent of 2M orders in one hour (about 8,000) were saved but never published, so no payment or shipping was triggered. Also, 150 orders were published but then rolled back in the DB because a later step failed. A reconciliation job found the gaps three days later.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: root cause, fix and prevention.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make Kafka more reliable" or "retry the send". The DB commit and the Kafka send are two systems; no retry makes them atomic.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do consumers deduplicate? Is ordering per order required? Do we have CDC (Debezium) available? What is the event volume?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Backfill: identify orders without a published event (join with a sent-events log or run the reconciliation) and republish them idempotently; also void or hold the 150 phantom events.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Dual write: save and send are not atomic; a crash or broker error between them loses or duplicates the event. (b) send happens before commit, so rollbacks leave published ghosts. (c) Producer settings (acks, retries) amplify it.
  4. How I'd verify each: Count orders vs published events by order id; check producer error logs during the restart window; check commit-then-publish ordering in the code.
  5. Root cause: No shared transaction between the database and Kafka. Two independent writes gave both a lost-event window and a phantom-event window.
  6. Fix: Transactional outbox: in the same local transaction write the order and an outbox row; a relay (Debezium CDC or a poller) publishes it and marks it sent.
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (...) VALUES (...);
INSERT INTO outbox (id, aggregate_id, type, payload) VALUES (...);
COMMIT;   -- relay reads outbox, publishes to Kafka, at-least-once

Delivery becomes at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent (dedupe on event id or a unique key). 7. Prevention: Reconciliation alert on order-to-event gaps within minutes, consumer idempotency tests, a lint rule against sending to a broker inside business transactions. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Outbox adds latency (poll or CDC lag) and a table to prune. Using 2PC/XA across Kafka is not an option. Do not publish before commit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Relay publishes the same event twice? -> Fine: idempotent consumers; keep event id stable.
  • Strict ordering per order? -> Key by order id and publish in outbox sequence.
  • Outbox grows large? -> Delete sent rows in batches or partition by time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team found a month of silent order gaps from a dual write; the outbox plus a reconciliation dashboard ended those tickets.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retry or "reliable Kafka".
  • Hire: identifies dual write and proposes the outbox with idempotent consumers.
  • Strong hire: backfill plan, ordering, cleanup, monitoring and why not 2PC.

questions.contextHtml: You are splitting a monolith. An order flow now crosses three services with their own databases: Inventory (reserve stock, 5 ms), Payment (external card charge, about 800 ms, 2 percent failure), Shipping (create shipment, 20 ms). Volume: 300 orders/s. The architect proposes XA two-phase commit across the three databases "to keep it ACID". Another engineer proposes a saga.
questions.promptHtml: Which do you choose and how do you design it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Saga is modern, 2PC is bad" without reasoning, or ignores what the user sees in the intermediate states.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the payment provider participate in XA (no; it is an external API)? Which steps are compensable (stock release yes; shipping cancel only before dispatch)? Is it acceptable for users to see "pending"? Why were the databases split: could the data stay in one DB?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; first consider whether keeping inventory and orders in one database avoids the problem.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) 2PC would hold inventory locks through the 800 ms charge: about 300 x 0.8 = 240 transactions holding locks at once, with blocking if the coordinator dies after prepare. (b) A saga commits each step locally and compensates on failure. (c) The payment gateway cannot join XA anyway.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype the failure paths: payment declined, service down mid-flow, duplicate messages; measure lock hold times.
  5. Root cause: The service boundary removed the single-transaction guarantee, so the choice is between blocking atomicity (2PC) and eventual consistency with compensation (saga).
  6. Fix: Orchestrated saga (Temporal/Cadence or a state machine) with steps: reserve stock (compensation: release), charge card with an idempotency key (compensation: refund), create shipment (compensation: cancel). Each step is a local transaction plus an outbox event. Order status moves PENDING to CONFIRMED or CANCELLED. A failed charge triggers "release stock".
  7. Prevention: Idempotency on every step and compensation, timeouts and a dead-letter path, dashboards on stuck sagas, chaos tests killing services mid-flow.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sagas have no isolation: another request may see reserved stock or a pending order, so design the UI and semantic locks ("reserved" state) accordingly. 2PC is only reasonable inside a platform that handles it (Spanner, CockroachDB). Splitting services is a one-way door in complexity; if data can live in one database with one shard key, do that.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Compensation itself fails? -> Retry with backoff, then alert and manual handling; compensations must be idempotent.
  • Two orders compete for last stock? -> Reservation is an atomic conditional update in Inventory.
  • Why not just retry the whole flow? -> Partial effects (charged card) need undo, not repeat.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team tried XA across services and hit stuck prepared transactions after a coordinator crash; the saga rewrite removed the blocking at the cost of an explicit PENDING state.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks by buzzword.
  • Hire: saga with compensations and idempotency, explains 2PC blocking.
  • Strong hire: lock-time math, intermediate-state handling, orchestration choice and an option to avoid the split.

questions.contextHtml: A payments ledger on Postgres has 4,000 commits/s at peak. p99 commit latency is 38 ms, mostly waiting on a synchronous standby in another availability zone (RTT about 2 ms) plus WAL fsync on a network disk (about 4 ms). The product team wants p99 under 10 ms and proposes synchronous_commit = off. Compliance says no acknowledged payment may be lost. Primary failure rate: about once a year.
questions.promptHtml: What do you recommend and what do you tell compliance?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Turns durability off for speed, or refuses any change without looking at where the 38 ms goes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which transactions need strict durability (ledger writes) vs which do not (audit logs, sessions)? Is the 38 ms mostly commit wait or queuing? What is the RPO (recovery point objective) for payments: zero?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed on production; first measure where time goes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The sync standby wait and slow WAL disk dominate. (b) Lock contention or connection pool queueing adds the rest. (c) Group commit is not batching enough because of low concurrency per connection.
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_stat_wal, wait events (WALSync, SyncRep), pg_stat_replication write/flush/replay lag, disk fsync latency (pg_test_fsync), pool metrics.
  5. Root cause: Durability costs one fsync plus a standby acknowledgment per commit; fsync on a network disk is slower than NVMe at 0.1 to 1 ms.
  6. Fix: Keep full durability for the ledger. Reduce latency by moving WAL to local NVMe, tuning group commit (commit_delay is a trade-off; verify benefit), placing the standby in a nearby AZ, and using synchronous_commit = off or local only for non-critical writes at the transaction level (SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off for audit-trail rows). Consider remote_write instead of remote_apply to shorten the wait.
  7. Prevention: Track commit latency percentiles and replication lag; document per-table durability classes; test failover to prove zero loss.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: synchronous_commit = off can lose the last few hundred ms of acknowledged commits on a crash (data stays consistent). With a once-per-year failure at 4,000 commits/s, that could be on the order of a thousand lost payments. I would tell compliance that the ledger stays fully durable and only non-financial writes may relax. A synchronous standby also stalls writes if the standby dies unless a quorum is configured.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Standby goes down? -> With one sync standby, commits block; use quorum (ANY 1 (s1, s2)) to keep going.
  • Multi-region? -> Cross-region RTT of tens of ms makes synchronous commit expensive; accept a regional sync pair plus async remote.
  • Could group commit alone fix it? -> It raises throughput, not single-commit latency, so only partly.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team turned off synchronous commit for a dashboard and found that a crash had also dropped recent ledger rows; they later scoped durability per transaction.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: turns off durability for everything or refuses to measure.
  • Hire: locates latency in fsync and sync replication and keeps the ledger durable.
  • Strong hire: per-transaction durability classes, quorum for availability, numbers for the risk, and a failover test.
